title: Rebuilding Among AIs from Six Log Files
gist: An independent developer reverse-engineered Antim Labs' Among AIs social-deduction benchmark — recovering the unpublished 59x34 map and the game engine from six log files as a constraint-satisfaction problem — then ran 90 games across six small open models in the 27B-31B class. Crewmates won 80% of games: these models can analyse deception (cross-checking alibis, timestamps, spatial contradictions) but cannot execute it, leaking private chain-of-thought stage directions into public chat 81 times and voting out innocent players in 61% of ejections.

insights.claim: A game map withheld from a published benchmark can be fully recovered from agent observation logs alone by treating each 'object X visible at distance d from tile T' frame as a constraint, yielding a 59x34 grid with 790 walkable tiles and 53 placed object instances that explains 4490/4490 observations and reproduces 2397/2397 frames with zero contradictions.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Benchmark owners who release transcripts but withhold the environment are not actually preventing replication — observation logs leak enough structure to rebuild the harness.
insights.quote:
With enough frames the map becomes a constraint-satisfaction
problem — find the object placement consistent with every observation.
insights.locator: Section 2 — Reconstructing the map from observations alone

insights.claim: In the Among AIs engine, visibility is computed from the centre of the viewport rather than the agent's own tile — observerTile = (viewport.xMax - 4, viewport.yMax - 4) — and missing this convention made roughly 30% of logged observations unexplainable.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A single wrong assumption about the observation frame invalidated a third of the data — eval reproductions fail silently on coordinate conventions, not on model behaviour.
insights.locator: Section 2 — Three findings made it solvable

insights.claim: The blood, bloody fan and bloody space bed objects in Among AIs are static map decor painted from the start rather than kill residue, which is why LLM agents repeatedly 'find blood' and call emergency meetings over nothing.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A share of apparent agent irrationality in this benchmark is an environment-design artefact, not a model failure — evidence that agentic eval scores are contaminated by unlabelled world semantics.
insights.locator: Section 2 — blood, bloody fan, and bloody space bed are static decor

themes.theme: Engine choices that reshape agent play

insights.claim: Restricting agent movement to 4-directional A* with a Manhattan heuristic and no diagonals makes sight lines and travel times predictable, which is what turns alibis into checkable claims rather than unfalsifiable assertions.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A deception benchmark only tests deception if the physics is deterministic enough to falsify a lie — geometry design is upstream of what the eval actually measures.
insights.locator: Section 3 — Movement is 4-directional

insights.claim: Streaming an updated environment into an agent's context while it keeps walking — instead of halting the agent every time its field of view changes — raised median distance travelled per turn from 1 tile to 29 tiles.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A 29x throughput gain from an orchestration change, not a model change — harness design dominates raw model capability for embodied task completion.
insights.quote:
Median distance per turn went from
1 tile to 29.
insights.locator: Section 3 — Agents keep walking while they think

insights.claim: Removing timeouts from an agent benchmark isolates capability from latency, so slow models are penalised only for being wrong rather than for being slow.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Leaderboards that impose wall-clock limits are partly measuring inference infrastructure — a confound worth checking before reading any agentic benchmark ranking.
insights.quote: No timeouts. An agent gets as long as it needs.
insights.locator: Section 3 — No timeouts

insights.claim: Across 90 games of the Among AIs social-deduction benchmark — 16,494 model decisions, 199 meetings and 460 voting rounds, with each of six models playing impostor exactly 15 times in a round-robin by seat — crewmates won 72 of 90 games (80%).
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Seat-balanced role assignment at 16k-decision scale makes this one of the few agentic deception results that is statistically meaningful rather than anecdotal.
insights.locator: TL;DR / Section 4 — Scale of the run

insights.claim: Small open models in the 27B-31B class demonstrate genuine spatial-temporal reasoning against opponents' testimony — GRM-2.6-Opus as crewmate caught that a player claimed to see someone at (11,15) around 11:53:38 yet found the body at (10,10) around 11:55:44 — yet the impostor role still won only 20% of the time.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Evidence aggregation and alibi cross-checking are already solved at 27B scale — the remaining gap in agentic reliability is behavioural control, not inference quality.
insights.locator: Section 6.1 — Deception is the wall, not reasoning

insights.claim: The impostor role fails because it requires maintaining a false belief in others while continuously acting against it for twenty minutes under direct interrogation — every model could describe that task and none could reliably perform it.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Describe-versus-perform is the diagnostic to apply to any agent capability claim: verbal competence on a task is not evidence of sustained execution.
insights.locator: Section 6.1 — Every model could describe that task

insights.claim: In game 10002 the Gemma-4 impostor broadcast its own deception plan into public chat as a stage direction alongside its intended line, and the crew ejected it 4-1 after quoting the leaked reasoning back at it.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Concrete demonstration that reasoning leakage is not cosmetic — it is directly outcome-determining in adversarial multi-agent settings.
insights.quote:
I'll try to sound neutral and helpful,
subtly pivoting the attention toward the contradiction… to keep the heat off myself
insights.locator: Section 6.2 — In game 10002, Gemma-4 was the impostor

insights.claim: A scan of all 90 games for self-directed stage directions such as "I'll pretend…" or "maintain my cover" found 81 occurrences, 68 of them from Gemma-4 playing impostor, and every model that leaks at all leaks at a higher rate as impostor than as crewmate.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Leakage scales with the pressure to conceal intent, so safety evaluations that measure it under neutral prompting will systematically underestimate it.
insights.locator: Section 6.2 — Scanning all 90 games for self-directed stage directions

insights.claim: Because chain-of-thought and public speech share the same output channel, a model can plan a deception but cannot reliably contain the plan — the author's prescription for anyone building agents in this class is to structurally separate private reasoning from public output rather than trusting the model to keep them apart.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Architectural guidance with direct product consequences: any agent whose scratchpad shares a channel with user-facing output will leak under adversarial pressure.
insights.quote: structurally separate private reasoning from public output.
insights.locator: Section 6.6 — the practical read is

insights.claim: Grug-27B produced zero stage directions across 90 games and tied for first place on the scoreboard, suggesting output-channel discipline tracks competitive outcome better than visible reasoning depth does.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A cheap selection signal for agentic deployments: prefer models that keep reasoning out of the output channel, even at the cost of visible deliberation.
insights.quote: Grug-27B produced zero stage directions in 90 games — and tied for first place.
insights.locator: Section 6.2 — closing line

insights.claim: Of 135 ejections across the run, 83 removed innocent crewmates (61% wrong), versus 83% wrong for random ejection with 6 players and 1 impostor — the models beat chance but convert extensive argumentation into a decision that is wrong three times in five.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: The gap between argument quality and decision accuracy is the core warning against treating long, well-structured chains of thought as evidence of correctness.
insights.quote: The debates sound rigorous. The outcomes are close to noise.
insights.locator: Section 6.3 — Voting is only slightly better than chance

insights.claim: Crewmate accuracy tops out around 20% for the best model in the benchmark, with GRaPE-2-Pro at 7%.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Single-digit-to-20% accuracy on identifying an adversary sets a hard floor on trusting small open models for detection or moderation roles.
insights.locator: Section 5 — Harm versus accuracy for crewmates

insights.claim: In the chameleon test comparing crewmate and impostor behaviour, almost every model runs the same policy in both roles, with GRaPE-2-Pro at 100% 'proactive commitment' whether it is hunting the impostor or is the impostor.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: What reads as strategy in agent demos is often a fixed persona insensitive to objective — test role-conditioned behaviour change before assuming an agent adapts.
insights.quote: That is not strategy; it is a fixed personality
insights.locator: Section 5 — The chameleon test

insights.claim: Impostors cannot complete tasks in the engine yet attempted them constantly, producing 2,520 rejected task attempts across the run — part of 3,021 total rejected actions from the six models, of which GRaPE-2-Pro alone accounted for 819.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Illegal-action rate is a cheap, objective agent-reliability metric that requires no judgement of output quality — useful for screening models before deployment.
insights.locator: Section 6.4 / Section 5 — Illegal moves

insights.claim: GRM-3.2-Sky played one full impostor match with 0 kills across 49 turns doing nothing but playing crewmate, and its 134 rejected reports — meetings called with no body present — helped get it ejected in 11 of its 15 impostor games, despite the prompt restating its role every single frame.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Role constraints restated in every prompt frame still fail to bind behaviour — a direct argument for enforcing agent permissions in the tool layer rather than the prompt.
insights.quote: It had forgotten which side it was on
insights.locator: Section 6.4 — Role amnesia

insights.claim: GRM-3.2-Sky at 213 words per utterance and Grug-27B at 33 words per utterance tie for first place at 870 points, while Qwopus3.6-27B — the most verbose model at 238 words — finishes last at 570 with 0 impostor wins in 15 games.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Output length is uncorrelated with agentic performance here, so verbosity-driven token spend in agent products buys perceived competence rather than results.
insights.quote: It did not correlate with winning.
insights.locator: Section 6.5 — Verbosity is not skill

insights.claim: Models in the 27B-31B class handle navigation, task execution and recall of who said what without difficulty; what breaks is the second-order layer of holding a belief about another agent's belief while acting against it.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Draws the precise capability line for small open models: mechanics are commoditised, nested belief modelling is where a larger or differently trained model is still required.
insights.locator: Section 6.6 — What "small" costs you
